subject: Biology
title: Organ Transplant Rejection
description: A 60-second lesson on Organ Transplant Rejection.

hook.text: A transplanted kidney is a lifesaver—but the immune system sees it as a foreign invader.

buildup.text: T cells recognize the donor organ's MHC proteins as non-self and launch an attack to destroy it.

discovery.text: Immunosuppressant drugs prevent rejection by dampening the immune response—but increase infection risk.

twist.text: Identical twins can exchange organs without rejection—their MHC proteins match perfectly.

climax.text: Scientists are engineering pig organs with human-compatible proteins to solve the donor shortage.

punchline.text: The immune system can't tell a gift from a threat.

quiz.question: Why do transplant patients take immunosuppressant drugs?
options: To prevent the immune system from attacking the donor organ
To speed up healing of the surgical wound
To prevent infection from the donor organ

details.summary: Transplant rejection occurs when the recipient's immune system recognizes donor tissue as foreign and attacks it. T cells identify mismatched surface proteins called HLA antigens on the transplanted organ. Lifelong immunosuppressive drugs are needed to prevent rejection.

takeaways: The immune system recognizes mismatched HLA proteins on donor organs
Patients require lifelong immunosuppressive drugs to prevent rejection
Closer HLA matching between donor and recipient improves transplant success

faq.question: Why do transplant patients need immunosuppressive drugs forever?
faq.answer: The immune system continuously patrols for foreign tissue. Without suppression, T cells would eventually recognize the donor's HLA markers and destroy the transplanted organ. Stopping immunosuppression almost always triggers rejection, even years after transplant.

faq.question: Why are identical twin transplants the most successful?
faq.answer: Identical twins share the same HLA genes and surface proteins. The recipient's immune system cannot distinguish the donor organ from self-tissue, eliminating rejection risk. These transplants require no immunosuppression, demonstrating the primacy of HLA matching.
